To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) the spatial distribution of animal‐transported active subsidies is fundamentally different from that of passive subsidies because animals respond to changes in the environment caused by active subsidies, 2) animal movement and ecosystem models can be used to predict the spatial distributions of active subsidies, and 3) this integration of animal movement and ecosystem modeling can provide a mechanistic understanding and improve predictions of active subsidy spatial distributions.

the spatial and temporal patterns of animal‐transported resources and how they are distributed across landscapes, which has important implications for the ecology and conservation of animals and plants.

the integration of animal movement and ecosystem processes is an important step forward in understanding active subsidies and the spatial distributions of active subsidies.

the ability to predict spatial distributions of active subsidies would provide useful information for ecology and conservation, and this can be accomplished by integrating animal movement with ecosystem models.

active subsidies are a unique form of subsidy that requires a new framework to understand their spatial distribution.

the spatial distribution of subsidy deposition by animal transporters can be predicted from the movement of the animals, the characteristics of the subsidies, and ecosystem responses to subsidy deposition.
